commit.message:
Promote registry 1.8.6 with the tested 3-CPU database quota (#1753)

Promote the search improvements from #1750 and #1752 as registry 1.8.6
and raise the PostgreSQL CPU quota from 1.5 to 3 on the existing
production nodes. Pool sizes, node count/type, memory and storage remain
unchanged.

Both migration 017 covering indexes were built with CREATE INDEX
CONCURRENTLY in production and verified valid, ready and structurally
correct; ANALYZE completed. The earlier migration 016 index is also
present and valid. A fresh pre-release database backup completed
successfully.

The combined application and CPU configuration passed two staging
repeats of 12,000 uncached searches, 30 full registry walks and 90
publishes with zero drops or request failures. Code alone at 1.5 CPUs
did not pass. See #1752 for full methodology and limitations.

Merge only after release artifacts/image are available and the full
production preview is verified. The singleton database will restart for
the CPU change. Monitor external probes, HTTP errors/latency, connection
queues, DB CPU/throttling and recovery throughout. If the new
application regresses, revert the image tag to 1.8.5 while retaining the
additional CPU budget and compatible indexes; reverting CPU would cause
another database restart.

commit.message:
Optimize broad searches and validate staging burst capacity (#1752)

Broad uncached searches consume the shared PostgreSQL CPU budget and
queue concurrent reads and publishes. Select matching page keys through
covering indexes before fetching payloads, and use parameter-specific
search plans so rare and broad terms do not reuse an unsuitable generic
plan. Filters, cursors, payloads and API page limits remain unchanged.

The tested fix also needs a 3-CPU PostgreSQL quota on the existing
nodes. This PR adds that optional setting and enables it in staging;
production configuration and the max 60/min 10 connection pool per app
remain unchanged. Query changes alone at 1.5 CPUs did not pass.

### Staging evidence

Using a fixed public production corpus, two app replicas and cold
ingress caches, repeated old/new/new/old trials at the same 3-CPU quota
showed:

| Trial | Searches completed | Dropped | Full walks | Publishes |
Publish p95 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Existing A1 | 11,762/12,000 | 238 | 30/30 | 90/90 | 604 ms |
| Candidate B1 | 12,000/12,000 | 0 | 30/30 | 90/90 | 290 ms |
| Candidate B2 | 12,000/12,000 | 0 | 30/30 | 90/90 | 450 ms |
| Existing A2 | 8,716/12,000 | 3,284 | 30/30 | 90/90 | 705 ms |

Both candidate repeats had zero request failures. All 83 complete
response hashes matched across 37 terms, both APIs, filters and
pagination. Both controls also had the new indexes; the control is
staging b96c5b2, including the earlier namespace fix, not production
v1.8.5.

The initial 100-second cutoff prematurely cancelled progressing full
walks even without searches. The repeated comparison extended only
observation to 180 seconds; search arrivals (200/s for 60 seconds),
publish traffic, crawl waves and per-request deadlines stayed unchanged.
Original failed experiments remain documented in [the full
results](tools/readbench/STAGING_SEARCH_RESULTS.md), alongside
machine-readable evidence and limitations.

### Validation and rollout

- Full internal/cmd race tests, deployment package compilation,
golangci-lint and `make validate` pass.
- Source-built Pulumi previews pass: staging changes the DB quota from
1.5 to 3 CPUs; production has no capacity change from this PR.
- Staging test workloads, diagnostic settings and benchmark rows were
removed; the previous app and 1.5-CPU quota were restored after testing.
Permanent node/ingress parity remains.
- No production writes, release or promotion were performed. Before
production promotion, concurrently build and verify both migration 017
indexes, then promote the application with the tested 3-CPU quota. The
current singleton DB restarts for a resource change; deployment
instructions document this requirement.

This establishes capacity for the specified burst and corpus, not a
guarantee for arbitrary future load.

commit.message:
Match staging compute and ingress topology to production (#1751)

Staging currently has two e2-standard-2 nodes and one ingress/cache
replica, while production has two e2-standard-4 nodes and two ingress
replicas. Those differences limit how confidently staging burst tests
predict production capacity.

Configure staging permanently with e2-standard-4 nodes and two ingress
replicas, retaining the existing two-node pool, 50-GB boot disks,
PostgreSQL limits/settings and application resources. Update the
deployment documentation to describe the shared sizing.

Validation: `make -C deploy build` and `git diff --check` passed.
Refreshed Pulumi previews for both stacks completed against isolated
copies of their checkpoints. Staging shows an update of the existing
node pool (machine type only), ingress scaling from one to two, and the
chart's corresponding PodDisruptionBudget; no cluster or node-pool
replacement. Existing Helm admission-hook/RBAC reconciliation also
appears. The production preview has no capacity/topology change from
this patch. Regional surge quota was checked and no competing GKE
operation was active.

Rollout recreates staging nodes using the existing surge policy, so its
single PostgreSQL instances can briefly be unavailable while volumes
reattach. The staging registry table has a verified production-data copy
and a retained logical snapshot. After staging settles, repeat the same
baseline/candidate burst tests; this PR does not release or promote the
application to production.

commit.message:
Optimize namespace searches and benchmark constrained burst traffic (#1750)

Namespace-spanning substring searches can make the trigram index examine
many candidates for very few results. Previously captured production
plans for `io.github.github/` examined about 133,000 candidates for one
row under both custom and generic planning. A local burst test
reproduced database CPU throttling, multi-second search latency, pool
contention and delayed publishing.

This change adds an index on the reversed, lowercased namespace and an
additional prefix predicate for searches spanning `/`. The existing
database name-format constraint guarantees exactly one separator. The
original complete `ILIKE` predicate remains, preserving case-insensitive
literal substring matching, partial namespaces, filters and pagination.
PostgreSQL's normal plan selection and pool/resource settings remain
unchanged. A custom-plan-only experiment did not solve the overload and
is not included.

The PR also introduces the previously prepared three-character minimum
in both API versions and the UI. **Compatibility:** nonempty
one/two-character or whitespace-only searches now return `422` before
service/database work; empty searches still list normally.

### Controlled evidence

The loopback-only runner uses 185,001 synthetic versions, two
apps/caches, and a Linux PostgreSQL container with verified 1.5-CPU /
4-GiB limits. Three cyclic crawler waves vary API version, page size,
query order and incremental watermark. Searches bypass caches, with each
category balanced across both replicas. Every trial offers 30 full
walks, 12,000 searches and 90 publishes; final order is A/B/B/A on a
fresh database.

| Measurement, range of two trials | Baseline | Candidate |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Complete walks | 18/30 | 30/30 |
| Successful searches | 7,514–9,075 / 12,000 | 12,000 / 12,000 |
| Driver-dropped searches | 2,914–4,483 | 0 |
| Full-name search p95 | 2,111–2,932 ms | 1.60–1.64 ms |
| Publish p95 | 452–591 ms | 12.09–12.86 ms |
| Database CPU over observation | 99.2–99.4 CPU-seconds | 37.2–39.5
CPU-seconds |

Both candidate trials completed every request without failures/drops.
Each variant completed all 90 publishes. The candidate served more
origin work while consuming less database CPU. Successful latency
quantiles are not presented as equal-work comparisons when the baseline
dropped work.

`tools/readbench/CONSTRAINED_RESULTS.md` and its JSON record final
results, exploratory controls, the corrected generator routing, and
limitations. Full response hashes match in 356 cases / 526 responses per
variant across both API versions. Earlier statistics/cache/cyclic
experiments remain documented separately.

### Validation and rollout

Passed full database and API handler packages against isolated
PostgreSQL; race-enabled search/benchmark tests, including
category/replica balance; repository-wide golangci-lint with zero
issues; `go build ./...`; `make validate`; Python and shell checks. The
fresh runner exercised migration 016 and cleanup end to end. All owned
services and the local VM were stopped.

Migration 016 adds the index (4.5 MiB on this fixture). For an existing
busy database, prebuild it concurrently, verify the exact definition and
validity/readiness, then analyze before deploying; `deploy/README.md`
documents the procedure. No production/staging release, migration,
configuration change or load test was performed.

The experiment establishes a local fix for the reproduced search-driven
overload, not that every historical alert shares this cause or that
production has a specific capacity multiplier. The synthetic mix,
architecture/storage and application CPU differ. Late queues cleared in
these tests, so a persistent post-burst stuck state remains outside this
proof.

commit.message:
chore(deploy): increase production PostgreSQL shared buffers (#1748)

Set production registry PostgreSQL `shared_buffers` to `512MB` using the
per-stack setting from #1747. Current incremental-sync traffic causes
substantial normal-buffer evictions and BufferMapping contention with
the default 128 MB pool; the servers relation footprint including
indexes and TOAST is about 299 MiB.

This isolates the buffer change. Production nodes remain e2-standard-4,
the app stays on 1.8.5, and CPU/memory resources, connection limits,
indexes, and cache policy are unchanged. It adds 384 MiB of configured
buffers and restarts the singleton database; rollback also restarts it.

Validation: all CI checks and independent review passed. The full
refreshed preview of head 83e34bf shows only `shared_buffers=512MB` plus
the acknowledged app deployment annotation, admission jobs, and Grafana
RBAC normalization. Staging deployment 40372902793 succeeded; SQL
confirms `512MB` with zero pending-restart settings, both app replicas
are ready, and direct listing, incremental-sync, and search smoke
requests returned 200. Staging nodes remain e2-standard-2.

Production memory peak is about 1.1 GiB against a 4 GiB limit with no
OOM events and ample node memory. The recent successful backup was
previously verified. After recovery/warm-up, compare 15 minutes of
workload-specific query rates, buffer evictions, waits, CPU pressure,
queues, errors, and listing latency. Restart-cleared backlog alone is
not evidence of a sustained fix.

commit.message:
chore(deploy): configure PostgreSQL shared buffers per environment (#1747)

Production incremental-sync traffic is causing heavy shared-buffer churn
and BufferMapping contention with PostgreSQL's default 128 MB pool. Add
an optional per-stack `postgresSharedBuffers` setting and exercise
`512MB` in staging before a separate production promotion. Unset stacks
retain the PostgreSQL default; node capacity, CPU/memory resources,
connection limits, and Grafana are unchanged.

Document memory budgeting, the singleton database restart, rollback, and
workload-aware verification. The production target is a buffer-only
experiment; it is not a claim that buffers alone resolve CPU contention.

Validation: `make -C deploy build`, `git diff --check`, independent
review, and all CI checks passed. Full refreshed previews succeeded,
including the committed staging head: staging changes only the intended
registry database parameter plus deployment housekeeping; production has
no database or node change. Production promotion waits for staging
restart, `SHOW shared_buffers`, and readiness verification.

commit.message:
chore(deploy): increase production node CPU capacity (#1746)

Production PostgreSQL is CPU-starved on its shared two-vCPU node. Set
`mcp-registry:nodeMachineType` to `e2-standard-4` for production only;
staging retains its `e2-standard-2` default from #1745. Keep two nodes,
application 1.8.5, PostgreSQL resources and buffers, connection limits,
cache policy, and disks unchanged.

The full production preview with workflow-pinned Pulumi 3.188.0 shows a
node-pool update (not pool replacement), plus existing deployment
housekeeping. The single registry/Grafana database instances will be
interrupted as nodes are replaced; ingress caches will also warm again.
Surge quota and the latest verified production backup were checked.

After rollout, verify node types, database readiness/reconnection and
placement, then compare CPU pressure, pool backlog, listing latency, and
errors under comparable traffic. A machine-type rollback is another
disruptive node rollout. Merge after the #1745 staging deployment and
final checks pass.

Production CPU contention requires additional node capacity without
increasing staging costs. Add `mcp-registry:nodeMachineType`, defaulting
to the existing `e2-standard-2`, so production can be promoted
independently in a subsequent configuration-only change. Neither stack
is resized by this PR.

Document node replacement, singleton database interruption, cold-cache
behavior, comparison metrics, and disruptive rollback.

Validation: `make -C deploy build`, `git diff --check`, and independent
code review pass. Full staging and production previews with
workflow-pinned Pulumi 3.188.0 pass and show no node-pool change.
Expected deployment housekeeping remains: the application
deployment-commit annotation, two recreated ingress admission Jobs, and
existing Grafana RBAC normalization. No database, disk, cache-policy, or
application-image changes.

commit.message:
chore(deploy): promote production to 1.8.5 (#1744)

Promote production from `1.8.4` to `1.8.5` to collect request
arrivals/backlog, database acquisition/query metrics, and bounded
per-request slow-listing diagnostics from #1742 and #1743. The
infrastructure deployment also appends cache status and upstream timings
to ingress logs.

The released commit is `ad119f3d478a936c95d73b291c5fbc106231f7bc`. This
release also includes publisher and validator fixes merged since v1.8.4.
No new database migration is included.

Validation:
- Diagnostic implementation CI passed, including integration tests and

commit.message:
feat(observability): diagnose individual slow listing requests (#1743)

Slow listing requests currently expose separate HTTP and database
histograms, but there is no request-level timing record. Database timing
also includes application JSON decoding, making a slow query
indistinguishable from slow row processing.

Add bounded structured diagnostics for GET `/v0/servers` and
`/v0.1/servers`: progress after 2 seconds and every 10 seconds while
outstanding, plus completion for slow or failed requests. Records
correlate ingress request ID, pod, route, query-shape flags, page size,
PostgreSQL backend PID and SQLSTATE, row/JSON-byte counts, and exclusive
handler/acquisition/query/fetch/decode/response timings. Raw SQL,
arguments, cursors, search strings and payloads are excluded. Logging is
capped per pod at 2 events/second with burst 10 and suppression
accounting; fast successful requests remain silent.

Validation:
- Full internal/cmd unit suite passed with race detection and coverage
against PostgreSQL 17.
- Controlled tests prove a blocked pool is visible before cancellation,
delayed queries are distinct from row processing, timings account for
the full request, and request IDs/context propagate through the real
Huma adapter.
- Tests cover SQLSTATE-only error detail, panic/cancellation completion,
timer shutdown and bounded log volume.
- `make lint`, `make build`, `make validate`, and `git diff --check`
passed.

Follow-up to #1742. No query, index, resource, or cache-policy changes.
After staging deployment, verify a bounded slow request and log
ingestion before cutting the production release. Internal PostgreSQL
wait attribution still requires contemporaneous database samples;
sampled logs are not exhaustive tracing.

commit.message:
feat(observability): expose request backlog and database waits (#1742)

When handlers stall, the existing request counter falls because it
counts completions, hiding incoming demand and backlog growth. Ingress
logs also omit cache outcomes, making duplicate upstream work difficult
to distinguish from database contention.

This adds application arrival and in-flight metrics, pgx pool
acquisition timing/pending counts and connection gauges, and query
timing after acquisition through row consumption. Database labels use
bounded operation/outcome values without SQL or parameters. Existing
completion metrics retain their semantics. Pool callbacks are
unregistered on close, and failed startup pools are cleaned up.

Ingress access logs retain their existing combined-log prefix and append
cache status, scheme/host, controller pod, upstream connection/header
timing, and a millisecond completion timestamp. The runbook explains
measurement limits, PromQL queries, and how to correlate cache and
database evidence. Existing log parsers anchored to the end of the old
format must accept the suffix; ingress logs remain in the existing GKE
logging destination rather than being added to VictoriaLogs.

Validation:
- Full internal/cmd unit suite with race detection and coverage against
temporary local PostgreSQL 17.
- New tests for blocked-handler arrivals, cancellation/panic cleanup,
canceled pool waits, query timing through row close, and bounded labels.
- `make lint`, `make validate`, `make build`, and `make -C deploy build`
passed.
- Local application smoke checks verified exported metrics for all four
list operation classes and in-flight drainage.
- GitHub CI passed, including the Docker-based integration tests,
build/lint/validation, govulncheck, and Go/Python/Actions analysis.

Application metrics require an application release/promotion; cache log
fields require infrastructure promotion. No changes to cache policy,
concurrency limits, SQL/indexes, or production configuration were
applied.
